newsitem.title: FRANCE: Memory of Cousteau honoured at Notre Dame mass.
newsitem.headline: Memory of Cousteau honoured at Notre Dame mass.

text.p: Thousands led by President Jacques Chirac gathered in Notre Dame cathedral on Monday to honour the memory of undersea explorer and environmentalist Jacques-Yves Cousteau, who died last week aged 87.
Cousteau will be buried on Thursday in a family plot in his native Bordeaux region in southwest France, ending a lifetime of wandering around the globe in search of knowledge and adventure.

The mass at the towering 12th century cathedral on the Seine River in central Paris was an honour generally reserved for heads of state. The last such ceremony took place in January 1996 after the death of former president Francois Mitterrand.

Cousteau's coffin was carried out of the cathedral into a waiting hearse by veteran crew members of the Calypso, the converted British minesweeper aboard which he shot "The Silent World", the film which first gave him world fame.
It had been brought in by an honour guard of French marines for a service led by Paris Archbishop Jean-Marie Lustiger.

"Jacques Yves Cousteau has gone with Jesus into the sleep of death," Lustiger said in his homily. "He made the world discover the immense universe of the sea. He was a poet who helped us to see an inaccessible part of reality."

Among those attending the mass were Chirac, members of the prestigious French Academy, which Cousteau belonged to, and anti-poverty campaigner Abbe Pierre, who for years had shared first place with Cousteau in opinion polls on the most popular figures in France.
Also present were several members of the French cabinet, Cousteau's children Jean-Michel, Diane and Pierre and ambassadors from nations ranging from China to Chili.
Chirac had mourned Cousteau as an "enchanter" and praised his pioneering films that explored exotic climes from the Antarctic ice shelf to coral atolls.

In one of his last campaigns, the outspoken Cousteau had joined international protests against Chirac's nuclear testing in the South Pacific in 1995-96. The island of Tahiti sent a wreath of flowers in a show of gratitude for his efforts.
Outside under a steady drizzle, hundreds of admirers had gathered to catch a glimpse of the coffin.

"His death made me very sad," said one man in the crowd of mourners, Louis Alleaum of Madagascar. "He is a man I have admired for a long time. For me, he was above all a sailor, the man of the sea," Alleaum told a reporter.
"He was a man who did great things for mankind," said Marie-Paul Draynville from Montreal. "It was he who warned us what was in store if we continued polluting."

During a lifetime devoted to environmental protection, Cousteau accused world leaders and business of irresponsibility and an obsession with money to the detriment of a clean and healthy environment, painting an apocalyptic picture of the gradual destruction of the planet and in particular its oceans.

A former navy officer who became an explorer, ecologist, filmmaker, teacher and millionaire, he also was co-inventor in 1943 of diving gear that freed undersea explorers from heavy helmets, allowing them to float in the water as if in space.
Cousteau's widow, Francine, has pledged to pursue his projects after his death.

She said last week her top priorities were to build a Calypso II to keep exploring the world as "a lookout to tomorrow's problems", and to start up a television channel called "The Human Voice" to record the culture and language of endangered peoples.
